planting.note: Set out grafted or air-layered trees in warm weather once soil has thoroughly warmed; because the species is typically dioecious, grow both a male and a female tree (or a self-fruitful selection) within pollinator range to get a crop.

directions: Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained tropical or subtropical soil, watering regularly while the tree establishes and reducing frequency once mature. Lovi-lovi bears its cherry-sized, deep red to maroon fruit directly along older branches and twigs in dense cauliflorous clusters rather than at branch tips, a habit shared with its Flacourtia relatives but with noticeably larger, juicier fruit than Flacourtia indica or F. jangomas. The tart-to-sweet fruit is eaten fresh once fully colored and softened, or cooked down into jams, syrups, and pickles that are popular throughout the Philippines and Malay Peninsula. Prune lightly after fruiting to keep the canopy open and encourage fruiting wood along the main limbs.
sources: Julia F. Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Transplant container-grown stock in spring into acidic, well-drained soil; in the southeastern US gulf coast this species has naturalized and is regulated as invasive in Florida, so check local rules before planting outside its native range.

directions: Grow in full sun to light shade on acidic, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil; the felted gray-green foliage and showy five-petaled pink flowers make this a dual-purpose ornamental and fruiting shrub. Flowers are followed by round, purple-black berries about a half inch across with a soft, sweet, slightly musky pulp that is eaten fresh, fermented into the Vietnamese rice-and-fruit wine known as ruou sim, or cooked into jam. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain a compact habit, and avoid planting where it could seed into natural areas, since it spreads readily by bird-dispersed fruit along the Gulf Coast.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Assessment of Non-Native Plants
USDA Forest Service Weed of the Week profile

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; this fine-textured form tolerates poor soil and coastal exposure better than large-leaved myrtle selections.

directions: Plant in full sun on lean, well-drained soil; this naturally compact, small-leaved form of common myrtle is denser and slower-growing than the species, making it a popular low hedge or container plant in Mediterranean gardens. Fragrant white flowers in summer are followed by abundant small blue-black berries that are the traditional base for Sardinian mirto liqueur and are also dried and used sparingly as a peppery, resinous seasoning for roasted meats. Harvest berries once fully dark and soft in autumn, and trim lightly after flowering since berries form on the current season's growth.
